A souvenir is an object you keep in order to remember a particular place, time, person, or experience.

The key thing about a souvenir is memory. It is not just any object — it is an object whose main purpose or value is to remind you of something. The thing matters less than the memory attached to it.

When you visit a new city and buy a small keychain shaped like its famous landmark, that keychain is a souvenir. You may never use it as an actual keychain. Its real job is to sit on your shelf and remind you, "I was there."

Three things usually come together:

  1. An experience or place — a trip, a concert, a holiday, a special occasion.
  2. An object connected to it — something you bought, found, received, or collected during that experience.
  3. The intention to remember — you hold onto it because it brings back that memory, not because it is useful.

Without that intention to remember, it's just an object. With it, it becomes a souvenir.

• A snow globe from Paris that you bought at the Eiffel Tower.
  • A seashell you picked up from a beach you visited on vacation.
  • A ticket stub from a concert you attended years ago.
  • A fridge magnet from a foreign country.
  • A small statue of the Taj Mahal bought in Agra.
  • A pressed flower from a garden you visited.
  • A T-shirt with the name of a city printed on it.

All of these are souvenirs because each one carries a memory of a specific place or moment.
Souvenirs Don't Have to Be Bought

Many people assume souvenirs are always purchased items from a gift shop — but that's not true. A souvenir can be anything you keep as a memory:

  • A pebble you picked up from the bank of a river you hiked along.
  • A dried leaf from a forest trail.
  • A napkin from a restaurant where you had a memorable meal.
  • A photograph printed and framed.

As long as the object serves as a reminder of a meaningful experience, it qualifies as a souvenir.

What counts as a souvenir is personal. The same object can mean very different things to different people:

  • A plain coffee mug is just a mug to most people.
  • But if you bought it at a café in a mountain town during a life-changing trip, it becomes a souvenir to you — because every time you use it, it brings back that memory.

The emotional connection is what gives an object its status as a souvenir.

Souvenirs are most commonly associated with travel, but they can come from any kind of memorable experience:

  • Travel: Buying a small ornament from every country you visit.
  • Events: Keeping a wristband from a music festival.
  • Relationships: Holding onto a cinema ticket from your first date.
  • Milestones: Keeping your graduation badge or a programme from a ceremony.
  • Childhood: A toy or object from your early years that you've held onto for the memories.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

• "She collected a souvenir from every country she visited."
  • "He kept the old concert ticket as a souvenir."
  • "The shop near the monument was full of souvenirs for tourists."
  • "That little bottle of sand is my souvenir from the beach trip we took ten years ago."
  • "They sold souvenirs outside the stadium after the match."

The plural form is simply souvenirs.
One Last Nuance: Value vs. Meaning

Souvenirs almost always have far more sentimental value than monetary value. A souvenir might cost almost nothing — a postcard, a pebble, a cheap magnet — but it can be priceless to the person who keeps it, because it holds a memory that no amount of money can recreate.

This is why people are often deeply attached to their souvenirs and reluctant to throw them away even when the objects themselves are worn out or broken.

In one sentence: A souvenir is an object — bought, found, or collected — that you keep as a physical reminder of a place, person, or experience that was meaningful to you.
